requirements.nl_text: Request Number - 6390 | Request Title - Notify sender if Signal message has been sent but not delivered to recipient after some time | Request Description - I have:   searched open and closed issues for duplicates  read https://github.com/WhisperSystems/Signal-Android/wiki/Submitting-useful-bug-reports  Bug description. Recipients who are registered for Signal may not be able to receive secure signal messages due to reasons such as:  temporary unavailability of internet access (e.g. prepay plans with hard data caps; otherwise intermittent data connectivity) permanent unavailability having uninstalled Signal without first unregistering Neither of these are apparent to the sender, and sending a Signal message results in the message sitting on the server for some undefined length of time. The sender does not get notified that while their message has been sent to the server, it has not been delivered to the recipient, leading to frustration once the fact is discovered ( #6377 , #2285 (comment) etc). The status is available in conversation UI in the form of one tick vs two ticks, but this requires the sender to explicitly check back in the conversation UI. It would improve the user experience if a signal message that was sent but not delivered after some timeout (minutes?) triggered a "lack of delivery" notification on the senders phone along the lines of "Your secure message to YYY could not be delivered after N minutes. Would you like to resend via insecure SMS?" This way it is up to the user to explicitly fall back to the less secure protocol. (This notification proposal is orthogonal to but complementary to the ability of Signal to better remember the per-contact preference of transport channel suggested in #2285 , #845 (comment) etc. It would also serve as an easier to implement and more secure alternative to automatically falling back to SMS as suggested in #678 , #2847 , #3074 , #4009 , #5001 )

requirements.nl_text: Request Number - 328 | Request Title - Feature request: Sending dummy short messages | Request Description - TextSecure could mask meaningful communication between people by occasionally sending dummy random messages to random recipients at random times:  Recipients would be chosen randomly between contacts that knowingly use TextSecure, so it could be recognized as such after decryption and automatically discarded by recipient. "Randomness" should be tweaked to level-out the legitimate messages, spoiling the traffic analysis of traffic retention data, preventing to weigh connections in the deducted social network graph or guessing sleeping/activity patterns. People often have many unused messages in their monthly quota, so those could easily be used with no extra cost, or they value their privacy more than some money. Sender would need to enable this feature (opt-in) and define desired quantity (eg max 100 dummy messages per month, 2 dummy messages for every legitimate one, max 500 messages total counting legitimate and dummy ones...). The feature would need to be aware of roaming (disabled by default, optionally enable) and battery level (do not send if bellow eg. 30%). http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_analysis#Countermeasures Possible extensions:  Recipients could be able to let their peers know, that they do not want to participate in this and do not want to receive messages for whatever reason (opt-out). Recipients could also be chosen randomly between other contacts (those not using TextSecure yet) to promote its use (default message) or a custom explanation by sender. Those messages would be in clear text. As this might be annoying it should be very limited (eg max 1 message to a single recipient per month, only during daytime...) to not be too intrusive spam. Dummy messages could contain other peer's phone numbers (random selection from those participating in dummy messaging, not just their contacts), never to be shown to user, just to send dummy messages to, to further mask the real social network. It would be tricky to opt-out later on once your number starts circulating, so opt-outs would need to be spread this way as well and by direct reply dummy message or by defining a TTL of each such number.

<MISSING_SCOPE>, if the user has switched on dummy messaging, then the App must send dummy messages to randomly chosen TextSecure contacts at random intervals.
<MISSING_SCOPE>, if the user activates "dummy messaging", then the System must periodically send "dummy messages" at random moments to random "TextSecure contacts".
requirements.llm_rimay: <MISSING_SCOPE>, if the sender has enabled the dummy messaging feature, then TextSecure must send dummy random messages to random recipients at random times.

verdict.text:
## Summary
Sonnet under few-shot reaches about 90% of the human-human similarity ceiling, matches every unit count, and passes Paska on 40 of 42 units. The main weakness is the condition slot. The model invents trigger clauses where the source states none (4 units) and drops conditions the gold contains (4 units). Two of those drops come from choosing different units than the annotators did.

## Missing-slot detection
Only scope (42 gold-missing) and condition (14) have support. Actor, modalVerb and action have zero gold-missing units, so their 0.0 scores are artifacts. The macro F1 of 0.34 is meaningless for the same reason. Use per-slot or micro scores instead.

Scope is handled almost perfectly. The only fills are both units of 5904-Signal, which suggests one source-level misreading rather than a general tendency.

Condition errors split evenly in both directions:
- **Invented conditions:** 1055-Signal#1 and #2, 226-Signal#1, 328-Signal#3. These recast the action's object or means as a trigger, as in "if a message is a draft" and "when the user opens the Android Context Menu". 328#3's "if the sender has enabled" is arguably grounded in the source's opt-in sentence. This is restructuring more than fabrication of new requirements content, but it still adds preconditions the source did not state.
- **Dropped conditions:** 1692-Signal#2, 1065-Signal#2, 6424-Signal#2 and #3. For 1692#2, one of the three annotators also omitted the condition, so the gold label is borderline.

With 14 condition cases, these 8 errors are too few to separate a systematic bias from noise.

## Conversion quality
The model sits about 0.05–0.08 below the human-human ceiling on all three similarity measures. The model's spread is wider than the humans' (seq_ratio std 0.17 vs 0.13), so the gap comes from a low tail rather than uniform drift.

The tail is concentrated in two places:
- **6424-Signal#1–#3** (seq ≈ 0.37–0.44). The model converted the worked search examples into units, while all three annotators converted the calling-code prepending rule. This is a disagreement over how to partition the requirement, not a wording difference. It also explains the condition drops on #2 and #3.
- **226#1, 6390#1, 6362#1** (≈ 0.44–0.48) make up the rest of the tail.

Paska found few smells, and both affected units are informative:
- **1065-Signal#1:** two actions packed into one unit. Under a fixed unit budget, the model merged content instead of splitting it.
- **328-Signal#4:** condition placed after the system response, and the condition itself is incomplete.

## Units and atomicity
Count compliance is perfect: 15 of 15 requirements returned the expected number of units. Non-atomic detection is trivially 1.0 because the prompt states the requirement is non-atomic, so it carries no signal here. Three requirements returned their units reordered; confirm that scoring aligns units by content rather than position. The 6424 case shows that a correct count does not guarantee the same partition as the annotators, and Paska's 1065#1 finding shows hidden merging within that count.

## Anomalies
- None.

## Next step
- Inspect the alignment for 6424-Signal and the 3 reordered requirements; if units are matched by position, re-score with content-based alignment.
- Tighten the condition definition in the prompt with a contrastive example showing that restating the object as a condition does not make it one.
- Compare this run against the zsl and cot runs on the condition slot before attributing the errors to few-shot prompting.
